A gland is an organ or a group of cells in a living body whose main job is to produce and release a specific substance. That substance is then used somewhere in the body — or expelled from it entirely. Think of a gland as a tiny biological factory: it receives raw materials from the blood, processes them, and outputs something useful.

This is the most important distinction to understand about glands. They are divided based on where their product goes after being made.

1. Endocrine Glands ("ductless glands")

These glands release their substances — called hormones — directly into the bloodstream. There is no tube or channel involved. The hormone simply diffuses into the blood and travels to distant target organs elsewhere in the body.

Think of it like a factory that releases its product straight into a river, and the river carries it far away to wherever it is needed.

Examples:

  • Thyroid gland (in the neck) — produces hormones that control how fast your body uses energy, your metabolism.
  • Adrenal glands (sitting on top of each kidney) — produce adrenaline (epinephrine), which triggers the "fight or flight" response when you're scared or in danger, and also produce cortisol, which manages stress.
  • Pituitary gland (at the base of the brain) — often called the "master gland" because it controls several other endocrine glands by releasing hormones that tell them what to do. It regulates growth, reproduction, and much more.
  • Pineal gland (deep in the brain) — produces melatonin, which regulates your sleep-wake cycle.
  • Pancreas (partially endocrine) — releases insulin and glucagon into the blood to control blood sugar levels.
  • Ovaries and testes — release sex hormones (estrogen, progesterone, testosterone) that govern sexual development and reproduction.

2. Exocrine Glands ("glands with ducts")

These glands release their products through a duct — a small channel or tube — that carries the substance to a specific surface or cavity, usually inside or on the outside of the body. The product does not enter the bloodstream.

Think of it like a factory connected by a pipe to a specific destination.

Examples:

  • Sweat glands (in the skin) — produce sweat and push it out through tiny pores onto the surface of the skin to cool the body.
  • Salivary glands (in and around the mouth) — produce saliva, which helps you chew, swallow, and begin breaking down food.
  • Sebaceous glands (in the skin, attached to hair follicles) — produce an oily substance called sebum, which keeps the skin and hair moisturized and protected.
  • Lacrimal glands (near the eyes) — produce tears to keep the eyes moist and clean.
  • Mammary glands (in the breasts) — produce milk after childbirth to feed a baby.
  • Pancreas (partially exocrine) — releases digestive enzymes through a duct into the small intestine to break down food.
  • Liver — releases bile (a digestive fluid) through a duct into the intestines.

3. Mixed Glands

A few glands act as both endocrine and exocrine at the same time. The best example is the pancreas: it sends digestive enzymes through a duct into the gut (exocrine function), while simultaneously releasing insulin and glucagon directly into the blood (endocrine function). One organ, two distinct jobs, two different modes of secretion.

The substances glands make are collectively called secretions. These include:

  • Hormones — chemical messengers that travel through the blood and regulate body processes like growth, mood, metabolism, and reproduction.
  • Enzymes — proteins that speed up chemical reactions, especially in digestion.
  • Mucus — a thick, slippery fluid that coats and protects internal passages like the throat, gut, and lungs.
  • Sweat, saliva, tears, milk, bile, oil (sebum) — various functional fluids as described above.

When people say "my glands are swollen" during an illness, they almost always mean lymph nodes — small, bean-shaped structures in the neck, armpits, and groin that are part of the immune system. Lymph nodes are not true glands in the strict biological sense because they don't produce secretions in the way glands do. They filter lymph fluid and house immune cells. However, "swollen glands" is a deeply ingrained everyday expression, and you will encounter it often. Just know the technical distinction: lymph nodes ≠ glands, even though they are routinely called that.

The word "gland" is also used in botany (the study of plants). In plants, glands are small structures that produce and secrete substances — for example, the sticky, hair-like glands on a sundew plant that trap insects, or the nectaries (nectar-producing glands) in flowers that attract pollinators like bees.

Outside of biology entirely, the word "gland" has a distinct mechanical meaning. In engineering, a gland (also called a gland seal or stuffing box gland) is a device used to create a seal around a moving shaft or rod where it passes through the wall of a machine or pipe. Its purpose is to prevent fluid (like water, oil, or steam) from leaking out around the shaft while still allowing the shaft to rotate or slide. You'll encounter this meaning in the contexts of pumps, valves, and marine propeller shafts.

A gland is an organ or cell cluster that manufactures and releases a specific substance. If it releases directly into the blood, it's endocrine; if it releases through a tube to a surface or cavity, it's exocrine. Some glands do both. Plants have secretory glands too, and in engineering, a gland is a sealing device around a moving part.
